newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tax deal won't hurt deficit target - sources.
newsitem.headline: German tax deal won't hurt deficit target - sources.

text.p: The German government's compromise on tax issues with opposition Social Democrats (SPD) will not impair its ability to meet the criteria to qualify for the single European currency, government sources said on Tuesday.

Germany's goal remains to reduce its budget deficit to 2.5 percent of total economic output in 1997, a comfortable margin below the Maastricht Treaty's 3.0 percent "reference value." Even if no further progress is made on tax points still left open, the deficit goal will be reachable, the sources said.
Some states' budget plans already show lower deficit projections than those they forecast in early summer, the sources said.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel and other representatives of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition agreed with SPD leaders late on Monday to set aside the most divisive aspects of the 1997 tax bill.

That decision will mean Bonn and the states have to find an additional 8.5 billion marks in spending cuts, as a wealth tax will be eliminated and state child support will be increased earlier than the 1997 budget foresaw.

The wealth tax brought states about nine billion marks a year, and the additional child support will cost 5.5 billion. Those losses will be partly offset by revisions to the inheritance tax and other changes.
Carl-Ludwig Thiele, chairman of the lower house's finance committee, said the elimination of the wealth tax was a long-overdue improvement that would make Germany more attractive to investors.
"This will reduce the cost of jobs, and set the stage for the creation of new jobs," said Thiele, a member of the Free Democrats, junior partners in the coalition.
The SPD's Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier said her party would continue to fight the elimination of the capital trading tax, especially now that the wealth tax had been done away with completely.
The issue was postponed once before, last year, and corporations will likely have to keep waiting for relief.
But both Matthaeus-Maier and coalition legislators said an agreement on inheritance tax was likely soon.
Party officials pledged to continue discussions on reforming corporate taxes, but conceded time was running short. Further talks will be held in the finance committee this week.
